planting.note: Broadcast seed in spring onto raw, disturbed, sandy or gravelly fill without deep burial; resents rich garden soil, which causes floppy, short-lived growth.

directions: A fast-growing, extremely low-water pioneer that blooms almost year-round from April into December, this plant is one of the most reliable late-season nectar sources in disturbed or restoration-style plantings and is useful for erosion control on raw slopes where little else establishes. It sends up a single camphor-scented candelabra stem topped in sticky yellow daisies. Best treated as a seed-bank species in a wild or restoration corner rather than a tidy border plant, letting it self-sow and roguing out individuals that stray into cultivated beds.

planting.note: Surface-sow in fall into loose, fast-draining dune or grassland sand in full coastal sun; skip summer water once established, since overwatering is the main cause of failure.

directions: A low, mat-forming coastal-dune native that flowers nearly year-round and tolerates salt wind, sandy soil, and neglect, this goldenaster is a useful low border or groundcover alternative to the taller, interior hairy golden aster already in cultivation. It forms a low, spreading silvery mat that holds its golden daisy flowers through most of the year, including winter in mild coastal climates. It is markedly more compact and mat-forming than interior golden asters, suiting rock gardens and dune stabilization.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall so seed experiences natural winter moisture before spring germination; site where soil floods or stays damp in winter and dries hard by midsummer.

directions: This goldenaster fills a niche none of the other golden asters cover — seasonally moist, clay-heavy alluvial and vernal-pool-margin soils along streambanks and washes — making it valuable for rain gardens, swale edges, and heavy-soil sites that stay wet in winter and bake dry in summer. Its bristly, variable foliage and yellow-centered flower heads make it less showy than other golden asters but valuable for naturalistic plantings in heavy or seasonally wet soils where true drought-only species struggle.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall with natural cold stratification into lean, rocky scree soil at elevation; best suited to Rocky Mountain rock gardens rather than mild lowland climates.

directions: A high-elevation, cold-hardy golden aster for Rocky Mountain rock gardens and scree plantings, this species fills a habitat and hardiness niche, montane and subalpine from 5,000 to over 8,000 feet, that none of the garden's existing warm-climate Heterotheca species serve. Reddish-green stems and bristly, long-haired leaf margins carry large yellow flower heads from June through October, later in the season than most montane wildflowers. Summer heat and humidity are its chief limiting factors in lowland gardens.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or spring with cold stratification into heavy valley clay; cut back old growth in late winter before new shoots emerge.

directions: The signature gumweed of California's Central Valley, this species is taller and showier than the coastal and prairie gumweeds already in cultivation, an important late-summer pollinator plant and larval host for Common Buckeye and Great Copper butterflies. Its large yellow flower heads exude a sticky white resin, especially in bud, that gives the genus its common name and was historically used medicinally by California Indigenous peoples. It thrives in heavy valley clay with no more than monthly summer irrigation once established.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or after last frost into dry grassy hillside or coastal bluff soil; self-sows readily.

directions: A shorter, deer-resistant, butterfly-attracting gumweed native to California and southwestern Oregon grasslands and hillsides, this species complements the coastal and prairie gumweeds already in cultivation with a distinct Bay Area and Coast Range ecological niche. It forms an erect, resinous perennial on dry grassy hillsides and coastal bluffs, producing branching clusters of yellow daisy flowers whose buds are coated in a thick, glistening white exudate. Its sticky, bitter foliage makes it markedly deer-resistant.

planting.note: Direct sow 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep in fall or spring into a rain garden or wet prairie site that stays moist well into summer, unlike most drought-adapted relatives.

directions: The dominant late-season bloomer across Pacific Northwest wet meadows, prairies, and upper salt-marsh edges, this gumweed fills a wet-prairie and salt-marsh-edge niche with no overlap among the dataset's existing, mostly California and Great Plains gumweeds. Resinous, sticky-based yellow flower heads open from midsummer into fall, feeding butterflies, native bees, syrphid flies, and wasps when many other Pacific Northwest prairie natives have finished blooming. An excellent choice for rain gardens and wet prairie restoration in maritime climates.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for winter cold stratification into sharply drained sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; withhold summer water except during establishment.

directions: A cold-hardy, strongly drought-tolerant interior gumweed of the Columbia Gorge, Great Basin, and northern Rockies, this species covers a continental-climate and dry-rocky-soil niche distinct from all the coastal and Central Valley gumweeds already in cultivation. It is a resinous, pleasantly fragrant perennial of dry grasslands, rocky outcrops, and streambanks, blooming its brightest gold in summer heat. It handles hard winters and wide temperature swings typical of the interior Northwest and northern Rockies far better than the California gumweeds.
